passages.happening:
The tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron. “Here we are, your own flesh and blood. Even in times past, while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back” (verses 1-2). And they remind him of what the LORD had said to him: ‘You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them’ (verse 2).

‘So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, where King David made with them a covenant before the LORD. And they anointed him king over Israel’ (verse 3).

The narrator gives the length of the reign. ‘David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years’ (verse 4): seven years and six months at Hebron over Judah, and thirty-three years at Jerusalem over all Israel and Judah (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of David's life. The boy Samuel anointed in secret, who waited through years of danger and would not take the throne by force, is now anointed by the whole nation. The division that followed Saul's death is over. It is about 1003 BC, though the dates are approximate.

‘Your own flesh and blood’ is in Hebrew your bone and your flesh, the language of family. The northern tribes are saying that David is one of them, not a foreign conqueror.

They give two reasons. David had led Israel's armies under Saul. And the LORD had chosen him to shepherd his people. Kings across the ancient world called themselves shepherds, but in Israel the picture carried special weight, because David had really been a shepherd and because the LORD himself is Israel's shepherd. A shepherd feeds, guides and protects the flock. He does not live off it. The word for ruler, nagid, stresses that David is appointed by the LORD: he is God's chosen leader before he is Israel's king.

Then comes the covenant. David does not rule his own people by conquest, but by a sworn relationship with them before the LORD, with duties on both sides. That principle set limits on royal power in Israel, even when kings ignored it.
passages.later:
The same words of kinship were spoken long before, when Laban welcomed Jacob: “You are indeed my own flesh and blood” (Genesis 29:14).

A psalm remembers the shepherd king: ‘He chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds’ (Psalm 78:70), and ‘So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands’ (Psalm 78:72). And Matthew, quoting Micah's promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, ends it with words close to the ones God spoke to David here: ‘who will be the shepherd of My people Israel’ (Matthew 2:6).
passages.asks: The tribes reminded David that his power was given to shepherd them. Ask whom you have been given some power over, at home, at work or in a church. And ask whether they would say you feed and guard them, or live off them.

passages.t: Jerusalem taken, and a palace built
passages.happening:
David's first act as king of all Israel is to march on Jerusalem. The Jebusites taunt him: “You will never get in here. Even the blind and lame can repel you” (verse 6). ‘Nevertheless, David captured the fortress of Zion (that is, the City of David)’ (verse 7).

David speaks of using the water shaft to reach the defenders, and the narrator adds a saying that came from that day: “The blind and the lame will never enter the palace” (verse 8). David lives in the fortress, calls it the City of David, and builds it up ‘from the supporting terraces inward’ (verse 9).

‘And David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him’ (verse 10). Hiram king of Tyre sends envoys with cedar logs, carpenters and stonemasons, and they build David a palace. ‘And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Jerusalem was a Canaanite city held by the Jebusites. Israel had never taken it for good in the days of Joshua and the judges. It sat on a narrow ridge, now called the City of David, south of the later Temple Mount, with steep valleys on three sides and the Gihon spring for water. It lay between Judah and the northern tribes and belonged to neither, which made it an ideal capital for a king of both. Taking a city and naming it after oneself marked it as the king's own, won by conquest and outside any tribe's land.

Zion is first named here, as the Jebusite fortress. The name later spread to the City of David, then to the temple hill, then to the whole of Jerusalem and to God's people.

The supporting terraces, the Millo, were probably stone terraces built on the slope to hold up buildings above. Archaeologists have uncovered a massive stepped stone structure on the eastern slope of the City of David, but its date and its relation to David are debated. The water shaft of verse 8 was long linked with a shaft Charles Warren found in 1867, but later excavations suggest that shaft was not accessible in David's time, and the Hebrew word itself is uncertain.

Hiram ruled Tyre, the great Phoenician trading city on the coast. He was also Solomon's ally, so many scholars think his help with the palace came later in David's reign and is placed here because it fits the theme.

Two sentences in the middle of the chapter explain the rest. David grew greater because the LORD was with him. And David understood that his kingdom was raised up for the sake of the people. The kingdom is God's gift, given for others.
passages.later:
The books of Joshua and Judges had recorded the failure: ‘But the descendants of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem’ (Joshua 15:63), and the Benjamites ‘failed to drive out the Jebusites living in Jerusalem’ (Judges 1:21).

Hiram's friendship lasted into the next reign: ‘for Hiram had always been a friend of David’ (1 Kings 5:1).
passages.hard:
What does the saying about the blind and the lame mean? Does it show contempt for disabled people?

Verse 8 is one of the hardest in Samuel to translate. The Jebusites mocked David by saying that even the blind and lame could hold him off. Many readers think David turns the taunt back on them, calling the Jebusite defenders themselves ‘the lame and blind who are despised by David’ (verse 8). On that reading, the words are aimed at the enemy soldiers, not at disabled people in general.

The saying that follows, that the blind and the lame will never enter the palace (in Hebrew, the house), may be a later proverb that grew from the event. Some connect it with the rules for priests, which kept a man ‘who is blind, lame, disfigured, or deformed’ from offering at the altar (Leviticus 21:18). Interpreters differ, and the Hebrew is uncertain.

What the wider story makes plain is this. A few chapters later David seeks out Jonathan's son, lame in both feet, and seats him at the king's table for the rest of his life (9:13). Whatever the proverb meant, the Bible does not treat disability as a reason to shut anyone out of God's grace.
passages.asks: David saw that he had been raised up for the sake of others. Ask what you have been given, and for whose sake. And ask whether there is anyone your own house, or your church, has quietly treated as someone who does not belong.

passages.t: Sons born in Jerusalem, and two Philistine defeats
passages.happening:
In Jerusalem David takes more wives and concubines, and more sons and daughters are born to him. Their names include Shammua, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon (verses 13-16).

When the Philistines hear that David has been anointed king over Israel, they come looking for him, and David goes down to the stronghold. They spread out in the Valley of Rephaim. David asks the LORD whether to attack, and the LORD tells him to go, ‘for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand’ (verse 19). David defeats them at a place he names Baal-perazim: “Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me” (verse 20). The Philistines leave their idols behind, and David's men carry them away.

The Philistines come again. This time the LORD tells David not to march straight up, but to circle behind them and wait by the balsam trees: “As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because this will mean that the LORD has marched out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines” (verse 24). David does as he is told and strikes them down from Gibeon to Gezer.
passages.hearers:
Kings of that world often took more wives as their power grew, many of them to seal alliances. Two names in the list will matter later, Nathan and Solomon.

The Philistines had crushed Saul. Now they move as soon as they hear that one king rules all Israel. The Valley of Rephaim lay southwest of Jerusalem, and these battles may have come before the capture of the city, when the news of David's anointing first reached them. The chapter is arranged by theme more than by strict order.

Notice how the two battles differ. The first time the LORD says to go up. The second time he says to circle around. David asks each time and gets a different answer. A victory last time is no guide to the next one.

Baal-perazim means lord of breaking through, and it plays on David's words that the LORD has burst out against his enemies. The same verb will come back in the next chapter, when the LORD bursts out against Uzzah. The power that breaks through for Israel is holy, and it is not to be handled lightly.

Carrying off an enemy's gods showed that the victor's God had defeated theirs. In the days of Eli the Philistines had captured Israel's ark (1 Samuel 4). Now Israel carries off the Philistine gods. The sound of marching in the treetops meant the LORD going out ahead of his army; the balsam trees are of an uncertain kind.
passages.later:
Chronicles adds what became of the idols: ‘There the Philistines abandoned their gods, and David ordered that they be burned in the fire’ (1 Chronicles 14:12).

The Gospels trace Jesus' family line through two of these sons. Matthew names Solomon, ‘by Uriah’s wife’ (Matthew 1:6), and Luke names Nathan, ‘the son of Nathan, the son of David’ (Luke 3:31).
passages.asks: David asked the LORD before each battle, even after a victory, and was told something different each time. Ask where you assume you know what to do because it worked before. And ask what it would look like to ask again.
